question: The primary purpose of high-lift devices is to:

options.text: Raise CLmax so the aircraft can fly, take off and land at lower speeds
Reduce induced drag at high speed

explanation: VS ∝ CLmax^−½. A higher CLmax lowers stall, lift-off and approach speeds, shortening ground distances; the price is drag and pitching moment.

question: Flaps raise CLmax from 1.5 to 2.4. At the same approach margin (1.3 VS), the landing ground-roll kinetic energy changes by the factor:
explanation: V ∝ CLmax^−½ = 0.791; kinetic energy ∝ V² → 0.625. Braking distance at a given deceleration scales the same way.

question: Flap extension raises CLmax from 1.5 to 1.9. The stall speed changes by:
explanation: √(1.5/1.9) = 0.889. The CLmax ratio itself (0.79) applies to V², not V.

question: Slats alone raise CLmax from 1.5 to 2.0. The stall speed changes by:
A Fowler flap extends the chord by 20 % (area referenced to the extended wing). At the same CL, the stall speed from the area increase alone falls by the factor:
explanation: VS ∝ S^−½: 1/√1.2 = 0.913. Deflection adds camber on top of this area gain.

question: A Fowler flap raises lift at a given angle of attack by:

options.text: Reducing wing area and raising speed
Moving aft to increase wing area and deflecting to increase camber, with a slot energising the flap boundary layer

explanation: Rearward travel adds area and effective chord; deflection adds camber; the gap supplies high-energy air to the flap upper surface.

question: A split flap (lower surface hinged down) compared with a plain flap at the same deflection gives:

options.text: Much higher CLmax with less drag
Similar or slightly higher CLmax with considerably more drag

explanation: The split flap increases effective camber while leaving a large separated region behind the upper trailing edge — a high-drag, simple device.

question: A slotted flap achieves a higher usable deflection than a plain flap because:

options.text: Air through the slot re-energises the flap's boundary layer, delaying separation on it

explanation: A plain flap separates at modest deflections because its boundary layer is inherited from the main wing. The slot starts a fresh, energised layer on the flap.

question: Double- and triple-slotted flaps are used on transport aircraft to:

options.text: Allow very large total deflection with attached flow on each element

explanation: Each slot restarts the boundary layer, so turning is shared among elements; combined with Fowler motion this maximises CLmax for landing.

question: Trailing-edge flap extension changes the zero-lift angle and the section moment coefficient as follows:

options.text: α₀ more negative; C_M,ac more negative (nose-down)
α₀ more positive; C_M,ac more positive

explanation: Flap deflection is added aft camber: both α₀ and C_M,ac become more negative, as for positive camber concentrated near the trailing edge.

question: On the CL–α curve, trailing-edge flaps:

options.text: Extend the curve to a higher stalling angle without shift
Shift the curve up/left and raise CLmax, reached at a lower stalling angle

explanation: Camber moves α₀ negative; the lift slope stays similar (slightly higher with Fowler area); the steeper recovery on the upper surface lowers α_stall.

question: On the CL–α curve, leading-edge slats:

options.text: Shift the curve left with lower stalling angle
Extend the linear range to a higher stalling angle and CLmax, with little shift at low α

explanation: Slats relieve the leading-edge suction peak; the curve continues along nearly the same line to a higher α before separating.

question: Flaps and slats deployed together produce:

options.text: A left-shifted curve extended to a higher CLmax than either device alone
The same CLmax as flaps alone
A lower stalling angle than flaps alone and lower CLmax

explanation: Flaps add camber (shift); slats protect the leading edge against the higher suction the cambered wing generates (extension).

question: Clean: lift slope 0.09/deg, α₀ −2°. With flap: same slope, α₀ −12°. At the approach CL of 1.2, the angle of attack with flap compared with clean is:
explanation: α = CL/a + α₀: clean 13.3 − 2 = 11.3°; flap 13.3 − 12 = 1.3°. At equal flight path, pitch attitude is lower by the same 10°, improving forward view.

question: With slats deployed, the stall angle rises from 14° to 22°. At the stall, the aircraft pitch attitude on the same flight path is:
explanation: θ = γ + α. The higher usable α is the price of slat-only lift gain — hence slats are combined with trailing-edge flaps to limit attitude.

question: A leading-edge slat increases the stalling angle because:

options.text: It reduces the angle of attack of the main wing
It adds weight at the leading edge
Airflow through the slot reduces the suction peak on the main wing and feeds high-energy air into its boundary layer

explanation: The slat carries part of the leading-edge suction; the slot jet reduces the main element's adverse gradient and energises its layer, delaying separation.

question: A Krueger flap is:

options.text: A panel hinged from the lower leading edge that swings forward, typically used inboard on swept wings
A fixed slot near the tip
A spoiler on the upper surface

explanation: It increases leading-edge camber and radius. Inboard Kruegers with outboard slats help ensure an inboard-first stall on swept wings.

question: A droop leading edge raises CLmax by:

options.text: Increasing leading-edge camber, reducing the suction peak at high α

explanation: The drooped nose aligns with the local flow at high α, lowering the peak velocity round the leading edge and delaying leading-edge separation.

question: Automatic slats on some light aircraft deploy:

options.text: Aerodynamically, when leading-edge suction at high α pulls them forward

explanation: At high α the suction near the leading edge overcomes the retraction force; at low α the stagnation pressure pushes them closed.

question: Asymmetric slat deployment at high angle of attack produces:

options.text: A roll toward the slat side
A roll toward the side without the slat, whose wing stalls first

explanation: The unslatted wing reaches its lower stalling α first and loses lift, rolling the aircraft toward it.

question: On a swept wing, slats are often placed outboard and Krueger flaps inboard because:

options.text: Stronger outboard stall protection ensures the root stalls first, avoiding pitch-up
Inboard slats would increase drag in cruise

explanation: Slats raise the stalling angle more than Kruegers; placing the more effective device at the tips makes the inboard section stall first.

question: Extending flaps changes (L/D)max and the glide angle as follows:

options.text: (L/D)max falls, so the glide becomes shallower
(L/D)max rises, so the glide becomes shallower
(L/D)max falls, so the glide becomes steeper

explanation: Flaps raise CD0 and usually k. tan γ = 1/(L/D): steeper descent at a given speed — useful for obstacle clearance on approach.

question: (L/D) falls from 12 to 7 with landing flap. The power-off glide angle changes from:
W = 600 kN on a 3° approach path. Thrust required with L/D = 8 compared with L/D = 12 is:
explanation: T = D − W·sinγ. W·sin3° = 31.4 kN. L/D 8: D = 75 kN → T = 43.6 kN. L/D 12: D = 50 kN → T = 18.6 kN. Higher drag keeps engines at a responsive thrust setting.

question: Flap extension increases induced drag at a given CL mainly because:

options.text: Lift is concentrated over the flapped inboard span, departing from elliptical loading
Flaps reduce the aspect ratio geometrically

explanation: Part-span flaps create a spanwise lift discontinuity, raising k (lower e); trailing vortices shed at the flap ends.

question: At the same approach speed, the rate of descent on a 3° path at 140 kt is about:
explanation: V·sinγ = 140 × 101.3 ft/min per kt × 0.0523 = 742 ft/min (≈ groundspeed × 5 in still air).

question: Small flap deflections compared with large ones typically give:

options.text: Mainly drag; large deflections add mainly lift
A good CLmax increase for a small drag increase; large deflections add mainly drag

explanation: Initial degrees of flap add camber efficiently; beyond moderate angles the lift increment per degree falls while form drag rises steeply — hence take-off flap is small and landing flap is large.

question: Extending trailing-edge flaps typically moves the wing centre of pressure:

options.text: Aft, giving a nose-down moment from the wing

explanation: Aft camber loads the rear of the section, making C_M,ac more negative.

question: Flap extension increases downwash at the tailplane. The effect on the tailplane is:

options.text: A nose-down contribution through the tail
A more negative tail angle of attack, producing a nose-up contribution
A less negative tail angle of attack

explanation: More downwash reduces the tail's α, increasing its download and the nose-up moment. The net pitch change is the balance of this against the wing's nose-down moment.

question: Extending flaps at constant attitude and power produces an initial:

options.text: Increase in lift (balloon), until speed decays and the aircraft is retrimmed

explanation: At fixed attitude and α, CL jumps; the aircraft climbs momentarily while added drag reduces speed.

question: Retracting flaps at low speed and constant attitude produces:

options.text: A loss of lift and sink, requiring higher α or speed

explanation: CL at the given α falls; unless α is increased (within the clean stall margin) or speed has increased, the aircraft sinks.

question: The aerodynamic load on an extended flap is proportional to q. Flying at 200 kt instead of 150 kt increases it by the factor:
explanation: (200/150)² = 1.78. VFE limits protect the flap structure and mechanism from this growth.

question: A flap load-relief system:

options.text: Extends the flap at high speed
Reduces flap drag at low speed
Retracts the flap automatically when airspeed exceeds its limit for that setting
Locks the flap at any speed

explanation: It prevents structural overload from over-speed with flap extended by moving to a lesser setting until speed falls.

question: Asymmetric flap extension (one side failed) produces:

options.text: A roll toward the side with more flap
Only a yaw away from the extended flap
A roll toward the side with less flap, requiring large lateral control

explanation: The fully flapped wing has more lift and rolls up. Most systems detect asymmetry and stop flap movement.

question: During a go-around, flaps are typically retracted to an intermediate setting first because:

options.text: It reduces drag while keeping CLmax margin at the current speed

explanation: Retracting fully at approach speed would put the aircraft near or below the clean stall speed (e.g. 1.2 VS,flap = 0.95 VS,clean for CLmax 2.4 → 1.5).

question: Stall-warning thresholds must change with flap and slat position because:

options.text: Each configuration has a different stalling angle of attack
Stall speed is independent of configuration

explanation: Flaps lower α_stall; slats raise it. An α-based warning uses a configuration-dependent threshold.

question: A take-off flap setting that raises CLmax from 1.6 to 1.9, ignoring drag changes, reduces the lift-off speed and ground roll (∝ V²) by the factors:
explanation: V ∝ CLmax^−½ = √(1.6/1.9) = 0.918; distance ∝ V² at the same mean acceleration = 0.842.

question: Take-off flap settings are smaller than landing settings because:

options.text: Take-off needs climb performance, which large-flap drag would erode
Large flaps cannot be extended on the ground

explanation: Take-off needs low V_LOF and a good climb gradient ((T − D)/W). Landing benefits from both high CLmax and high drag for a steep, slow approach.

question: At a high-elevation hot aerodrome with limited climb performance, a lower flap setting for take-off:

options.text: Lowers V_LOF and reduces climb gradient
Shortens the runway required and improves climb
Raises lift-off speed and runway length but improves the climb gradient

explanation: Less flap → lower CLmax → higher V_LOF → longer run; less drag → higher (T − D)/W. The optimum depends on whether runway or obstacle limits.

question: Landing speed 160 kt reduced to 140 kt by higher flap. Energy to be absorbed on the runway changes by:
Flap extension reduces the landing distance mainly because:

options.text: Lower approach and touchdown speed (kinetic energy ∝ V²) and higher drag

explanation: Lower V_ref cuts energy by the square of the speed ratio; aerodynamic drag contributes to deceleration in the flare and early roll.

question: With trailing-edge flaps extended at a fixed CL, the stall margin in angle of attack terms:

options.text: Is reduced, because the stalling angle is lower

explanation: Flaps lower α_stall. Speed margin is preserved by scheduling speeds on the flap stall speed, but α margin shrinks.

question: Compared with a plain flap, the CLmax gain of a Fowler flap is larger because:

options.text: It adds wing area and a slot in addition to camber

explanation: Area increase raises lift at equal CL; the slot permits larger effective camber; both add to CLmax referenced to the original area.

question: A Gurney flap (small tab normal to the lower trailing edge):

options.text: Acts only as a speed brake
Increases effective camber, raising CL at given α and CLmax, with a drag increment

explanation: The tab alters the trailing-edge flow, shifting the rear stagnation point and producing extra circulation — a small, fixed high-lift aid.

question: The slot of a slatted wing is most effective:

options.text: At high angles of attack, where the main element's leading-edge suction peak is severe
In cruise at high Mach number

explanation: At low α the slot contributes little and adds drag; at high α it relieves the peak and energises the layer, delaying the stall.

question: Vortex generators ahead of the ailerons improve low-speed handling by:

options.text: Keeping outboard flow attached at higher α, preserving aileron authority
Reducing the stall speed of the root

explanation: Streamwise vortices transfer momentum toward the wall, delaying separation over the control surface.

question: Boundary-layer control by blowing or suction raises CLmax by:

options.text: Delaying separation at high α or on deflected flaps

explanation: Suction removes low-energy fluid; blowing adds momentum. Either lets the flow negotiate larger pressure recoveries.

question: Increasing CLmax by 30 % at constant approach margin reduces the approach speed by about:
Spoilers deployed in flight (speed brake) compared with clean:

options.text: Increase drag and reduce CLmax, raising the stall speed
Have no effect on stall speed

explanation: Spoilers spoil upper-surface lift over part of the span and add form drag; the reduced CLmax means a higher VS while deployed.

question: Ground spoilers deployed at touchdown improve braking because:

options.text: They dump lift, transferring weight onto the wheels, and add drag

explanation: Braking force = μ·(W − L). Reducing L raises the wheel load and the available friction force.

question: Flaps in the take-off setting change the lift-curve slope relative to clean mainly through:

options.text: Fowler area gain (slope referenced to the original area rises slightly)

explanation: Camber alone leaves the slope unchanged; extending chord increases lift per degree referenced to the nominal area.

question: The pitch change on flap extension in a given aircraft depends on:

options.text: The balance between wing C_M,ac change and the change in tailplane downwash

explanation: Aft camber adds nose-down wing moment; increased downwash reduces tail α (nose-up). Tail height and position decide which dominates.

question: Extending flaps above VFE risks:

options.text: Structural overload of the flap and its mechanism

explanation: Air loads grow with q; VFE is set by the flap structure, not by aerodynamic performance.

question: With landing flap, the aircraft touches down at a lower pitch attitude than with less flap because:

options.text: The required CL is reached at a lower angle of attack

explanation: Camber reduces the α for a given CL; for the same flight path and speed margin, attitude is lower (better view, tail clearance).

question: Slats deployed at high cruise speed would mainly:

options.text: Add drag with no benefit, and are limited by a maximum extension speed

explanation: Slats help only at high α; at low α they add parasite drag and structural load, so they are retracted in cruise.

question: Clean CLmax 1.5 at α 15°. Flaps raise CLmax to 2.2 at α 12°. At 1.3 VS in each configuration, CL is:
High-lift devices compared with a larger fixed wing area for the same low-speed CLmax:

options.text: Give low stall speed without the cruise drag and weight of a larger wing
Are always lighter and add no drag

explanation: A larger wing would carry its wetted area and weight into cruise, where CL is low; retractable devices provide lift only when needed.

question: The drag curve with landing flap compared with clean (same weight) is:

options.text: Higher and shifted to higher speed
Lower and shifted to higher speed
Higher and shifted to lower speed

explanation: CD0 rises (curve up); V_md ∝ (k/CD0)^¼ falls (left). Minimum drag speed and stall speed both decrease.

question: Flap extension in a turn at constant speed and bank:

options.text: Has no effect on stall margin
Increases the stall margin in speed terms but reduces it in angle-of-attack terms
Reduces the stall speed and raises the stalling angle

explanation: VS falls (larger speed margin) while α_stall falls. The load factor is unchanged by flap; CL demand is reached at a lower α.

question: Increasing flap deflection beyond the optimum produces:

options.text: Little further CLmax gain, flap-surface separation and a steep rise in drag

explanation: Beyond the angle at which the flap boundary layer can stay attached, extra deflection separates the flap and adds pressure drag.
